newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro could cut forex volume by $90 bln/day - banker.
newsitem.headline: Euro could cut forex volume by $90 bln/day - banker.

text.p: Foreign exchange business in the future EMU zone could contract by 20 percent, or $90 billion a day, after the launch of the single European currency, the Luxembourg Bankers' Association chairman said on Friday.
Association chairman Paul Meyers said in a speech: "There are at least four reasons which prevent bankers from welcoming the euro with open arms" in the European Union.

He listed the cost of changing technical systems, a reduction in the volume of currency dealing, lower interest rates and margins resulting from economic convergence criteria between EU members, and increased competition as globalisation quickened.
"The losses which banks are expecting on exchange transactions after the disappearance of national (EU) currencies clearly illustrate bankers' fears," Meyers said.
"The Belgians expect a 60 percent earnings loss on foreign exchange business, and the French and Germans 25 percent," he said.
"If we are to believe the experts, the volume of exchange business will fall by one-fifth overall in the euro zone, representing the appreciable amount of $90 billion every day."
He said the dissolution of EU currencies would significantly limit euromarket activity, where Luxembourg banks have a 12 percent share.

"Although it is hard to predict how rates and consequently margins will develop, we must expect, at least in the immediate future, the contraction of the euromarkets to affect bank earnings, two-thirds of which are accounted for by income from margins," Meyers said.

In capital markets, he said the disappearance of the Luxembourg franc would seriously impact earnings because of the importance of Luxembourg franc-denominated bond issues. The issues increased by 500 percent to 420 billion francs in the six years to 1995.

The transition to a single currency in Europe could cause a disappearance of investment funds. Meyers noted there had been a 10-fold increase in the number of funds in 10 years, with assets now totalling $330 billion, ranking Luxembourg fourth among world centres of the fund industry.

"This proud achievement might be affected by the introduction of the single currency because of the disappearance of bond funds and monetary funds denominated in those European currencies which will disappear," he said.
Meyers said Luxembourg banks would need to invest eight to 10 billion francs in the technical transition to the euro.
